title: The Dancing Girl of Izu
significance: The story follows, without incident, a few days in which a high-school-age narrator walks the Izu Peninsula alongside a troupe of traveling performers. It is the short story in which Kawabata's narration — rendering feeling only through changes in weather, sound, and distance rather than statement — first reached its finished form.

title: Snow Country
significance: A novel that began as a magazine serial in 1935, passed through a single-volume edition in 1937, and was not completed until 1948. Set on the closed stage of a snowbound hot-spring town, it advances the relationship between a man from Tokyo and a geisha through changes of season and distance rather than through incident.

title: Thousand Cranes
significance: Using the implements and etiquette of the tea ceremony as the medium for relationships among its characters, it narrates how a relationship from the father's generation carries over intact into the son's generation, told through the history of a single tea bowl.

title: The Sound of the Mountain
significance: Narrated from the vantage of an aging company employee watching his son's marriage come apart beside him, the novel fixes the approach of death in a single auditory image: the sound of the mountain heard at night.

title: House of the Sleeping Beauties
significance: Set in a house of business where old men spend the night beside women put to sleep by drugs, this novella leaves only a relationship without exchanged words, pushing the narration of sensation and memory as far as it will go.

title: Bannen
significance: The story collection Dazai assembled as his first book. Under a title he meant as a suicide note, it gathers early work in which he tested how to write his own story, changing narrator and form from piece to piece.

title: Run, Melos!
significance: The story of a man running back to keep his promise, it takes an exceptionally straightforward narrative form within a body of work otherwise dominated by self-destructive narrators. Long included in Japanese school textbooks, it is the best known of his short stories.

title: The Setting Sun
significance: Narrated by the daughter of an aristocratic family in decline after Japan's defeat, it records the breakup of the class system. The novel gave rise to the catchphrase 'the setting-sun tribe' and shaped how postwar Japanese society understood itself.

title: Villon's Wife
significance: Narrated from the wife's point of view, it tells how the wife of a poet pursued by drinking debts takes a job at a bar herself and shoulders the household. It is one of the rare Dazai stories that views a collapsing man from the outside.

title: No Longer Human
significance: Built from three notebooks and a frame narrator who introduces them, it presents, in the form of a document, a confession of having failed to perform being human. Serialization began just before Dazai's death, and the final installment appeared posthumously.

title: Confessions of a Mask
significance: A first-person novel in which a narrator who has performed normalcy over his attraction to other men lays out, in order, the history of that performance. It is the first work through which Mishima won a place in the postwar literary world.

title: The Sound of Waves
significance: A love story that transplants the structure of the Greek classic Daphnis and Chloe onto a small island in Ise Bay. Among Mishima's novels it has the least intrusion of abstract ideas and the shortest sentences.

title: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion
significance: It reconstructs the actual 1950 arson of the Golden Pavilion through the first-person account of a stuttering acolyte. The claim that beauty blocks life is carried forward not by the causal chain of events but by the narrator's argument.

title: Five Modern Noh Plays
significance: A collection of plays that transposes classic Noh works into spoken drama set in the contemporary city. Keeping the structure of the original pieces while changing only setting and characters, it tested whether a traditional dramatic form could still work on the contemporary stage.

title: The Sea of Fertility
significance: A tetralogy that began serialization in 1965 and was completed in 1971. Taking as its organizing principle the premise that one figure is reborn across generations, it divides sixty years of twentieth-century Japan into four volumes by era. The manuscript of the final volume was handed over on the morning of the author's death, and the fourth volume was published posthumously.

title: Kabe
significance: An early story collection whose title piece follows a man who has lost his own name being pushed aside, in turn, by objects and events. With the included story 'The Crime of Mr. S. Karma,' Abe won the Akutagawa Prize and gained a place in the literary world.

title: Inter Ice Age 4
significance: A novel that opens as a machine built to predict the future calculates its own developer's fate. Premised on the re-engineering of humanity after a rise in sea level, it is counted as an early example of the Japanese-language SF novel.

title: The Woman in the Dunes
significance: It narrates how a teacher out collecting insects is trapped in a house at the bottom of a sand pit and drawn into the daily labor of shoveling sand. Hiroshi Teshigahara's 1964 film brought it international recognition.

title: The Face of Another
significance: It records, in the form of notebooks the man leaves behind, how a man disfigured by burns to his face builds an elaborate mask and approaches his own wife under another identity.

title: Friends
significance: A play in which a family of strangers moves into the home of a man living alone and, in the name of goodwill, begins to take charge of his life. It is a key work showing that Abe's plays share the same experiments with premise as his novels.

title: The Box Man
significance: The notebooks of a man who wanders the city with a cardboard box over his head are overlaid with the records of other narrators, in a structure where who is doing the writing is never settled.

title: Prize Stock
significance: A short story, told from a boy's point of view, about the days during which a mountain village cages a Black American soldier who has crash-landed nearby, as if he were livestock. It won the Akutagawa Prize, and it is here that the valley-village setting Oe would return to repeatedly first appears.

title: A Personal Matter
significance: It follows a few days in the life of a father contemplating flight in the face of a child born with a head deformity. It is the turning point at which Oe drew his own experience in as a condition of the novel.

title: Hiroshima Notes
significance: A record of repeated reporting trips to Hiroshima, in which Oe met with atomic-bomb survivors and their doctors. By narrating the bomb not as a symbol but as an ongoing problem of treatment and administration, it opened Oe's line of social essays.

title: The Silent Cry
significance: A novel that overlays the story of two brothers returning to a Shikoku valley with a peasant uprising of 1860, superimposing two rebellions a hundred years apart onto the same terrain. It won the Tanizaki Jun'ichiro Prize.

title: Moeagaru Midori no Ki
significance: Across three volumes it narrates the formation and collapse of a new religious community that arises in a Shikoku valley. It was published between 1993 and 1995, and Oe once described it as his last novel.

title: Love in a Fallen City
significance: A novella in which the give-and-take between a divorced woman and an overseas-Chinese businessman in Hong Kong is finally resolved into marriage by the Pacific War's fall of Hong Kong. The irony that a marriage can only succeed once a whole city has fallen is representative of Eileen Chang's method.

title: The Golden Cangue
significance: It narrates thirty years in which a woman sold into a family of herbal-medicine merchants guards her property while ruining her children's lives one after another. C. T. Hsia named it a leading example of the modern Chinese novella, and it became the basis for Eileen Chang's critical reevaluation.

title: Written on Water
significance: A collection of essays on clothes, food, neighbors, and film. Recording wartime life in Shanghai without recourse to political language, it shows in prose the same density of observation found in the fiction.

title: The Rice-Sprout Song
significance: A novel dealing with rural hunger and requisitioning after land reform. Written on commission from the United States Information Service while Chang was living in Hong Kong, it appeared first in a Chinese edition and then in the author's own English version.

title: Lust, Caution
significance: A short story about a student cell plotting to assassinate the intelligence chief of a Japanese-collaborationist regime, and the operative whose resolve wavers mid-mission. Chang conceived it in the 1950s but published it only after some twenty years of revision.

title: Kali Shalwar
significance: It follows a few days in which a prostitute who has moved to Delhi tries to get hold of a black shalwar to wear for a holiday. It shows an early version of Manto's method of revealing a character's situation only through the transaction over a single object, without explanation, and it is one of the stories for which he was charged with obscenity.

title: Open It
significance: A story of only a few pages in which a father who lost his daughter on a refugee train asks a search party to find her, and is reunited with her at a hospital. Its final two sentences invert the nature of what has happened, and the magazine that ran it was suspended shortly after publication.

title: Black Margins
significance: A collection of vignettes, each cut down to three or four lines or little more than a page, on the looting and killing of the Partition period. Stripping away all commentary and expressed emotion to leave only action, it makes the reader laugh and then retrace what, exactly, they were laughing at.

title: Colder Than Ice
significance: A story in which a man who took part in the rioting confesses to his wife what he did. Charged with obscenity in Pakistan, it became the longest-contested of Manto's trials.

title: Letters to Uncle Sam
significance: A series of open letters addressed, in form, to the United States as 'Uncle Sam.' Written in a tone that mocks Cold War-era American military aid to Pakistan, nine letters were published between 1951 and shortly before Manto's death.

title: Toba Tek Singh
significance: A few years after Partition, the two countries agree to exchange asylum inmates by religion, and a man who never manages to confirm which side his hometown now belongs to is left standing on the border line itself. It appeared in a story collection in 1955, the year Manto died.

title: Swami and Friends
significance: Narayan's first novel, following ten-year-old Swami through his school and its back lanes, and the work in which Malgudi first appears. It was published after Graham Greene, at a point when no one would take the manuscript, arranged a British publisher for it.

title: The English Teacher
significance: A novel in which a college English lecturer loses his wife to typhoid, then moves in its second half toward trying to continue speaking with her through séances. It is known as the work into which Narayan's own experience of bereavement entered directly.

title: The Financial Expert
significance: It follows Margayya, who sits under a banyan tree brokering loans, as he builds up a fortune and then loses it. The novel narrates the economy of Malgudi through the ledger of a single man.

title: The Guide
significance: It crosscuts present-day scenes in the village with flashback as it tells the story of a tourist guide who passes through prison, is mistaken for a holy man, and finally undertakes a fast. It won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960.

title: The Man-Eater of Malgudi
significance: A taxidermist moves into the attic of a mild-mannered printer and throws the town into turmoil. It transposes the Hindu myth of Bhasmasura onto the scale of small-town daily life.

title: My Days: A Memoir
significance: A memoir Narayan wrote himself, covering the years from childhood to his establishment as a writer. It is a primary account of how Malgudi was conceived and of his early publishing history.

title: The Age of Doubt
significance: A short story following the deceptions a woman who lost her husband and son in the war encounters at a hospital and a temple. It won the 1957 newcomer's prize from the literary magazine Hyundae Munhak and made Park Kyong-ni's name known.

title: Pyoryudo
significance: Set in a Seoul where a woman widowed by the war makes her living running a tearoom, it is an early novel that takes head-on the economics and gossip surrounding a woman living on her own.

title: The Curse of Kim's Daughters
significance: It narrates, on the timeline of a household, how the lives of the daughters of a Tongyeong herbal-medicine family go wrong one after another. Among Park Kyong-ni's novels before Land, it was the most widely read and has been adapted for film and television several times.

title: Sijang gwa Jeonjang
significance: A novel that splits the Korean War into two axes — the life of the marketplace and the ideology of the battlefield — and narrates them in counterpoint. It placed its leftist characters as people living their lives rather than as instruments of ideology.

title: Land
significance: A multigenerational saga that took twenty-five years to complete, from the start of its serialization in the magazine Hyundae Munhak in 1969 to the completion of its fifth part in 1994. Starting from the Choi family of Pyeongsari, Hadong, in the last years of the Korean Empire, it follows the generation of Seo-hui and Gilsang as the setting moves through Jinju, Gando (Jiandao), and Tokyo, narrating the entire colonial period through a genealogy of characters.
